analysis.one_liner: Lets banks buy banks and open branches in other states, dismantling decades-old geographic barriers.
analysis.headline: The Senate folded this bill into H.R. 3841 and passed it by voice vote on April 26, 1994; interstate banking became federal law later that year.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill lets large banking companies that meet capital and management standards buy banks in any state, whether or not the state wants them, and merge their banks in different states into a single bank with branches nationwide. States keep some tools: they can tax out-of-state branches, apply their consumer-protection and fair-lending laws, and opt out of some combinations. The bill also requires federal regulators to grade interstate banks' Community Reinvestment Act record state by state.
analysis.who_benefits: Large bank holding companies and national banks gain the right to acquire banks and operate branches across state lines — the goal the biggest banks had pursued for years. Bank customers gain access to wider branch networks and can keep accounts while moving. Communities keep some protections: federal regulators must evaluate an interstate bank's community lending record separately in each state, and no single company may hold more than 10% of the nation's deposits or 25% of one state's deposits.

how_it_helps.text: Lets adequately capitalized, adequately managed bank holding companies acquire existing banks in other states even if the host state's law forbids it, subject to a 10% national deposit cap and a 25% state cap.
Lets a holding company with banks in several states combine them into a single bank that operates the old offices as branches, expanding branching nationwide.

Lets a state opt in to interstate branching by national and state banks, and lets host states tax out-of-state banks' shares and apply their own consumer-protection, fair-lending, and community reinvestment laws to the new branches.

Requires federal regulators to write separate Community Reinvestment Act evaluations of an interstate bank's performance in each state and in multistate metro areas, so local lending records stay visible.

Preserves federal and state antitrust laws and lets host states opt out of interstate combinations, and keeps the authority of state examiners over out-of-state branches through cooperative agreements.
Reduces from two-thirds to a majority the share of a national bank's directors who must reside in the bank's state, easing out-of-state control.

analysis.who_pays: Communities that lose locally owned banks: acquisition and branching pressure pushes ownership and lending decisions out of state, and history shows consolidation followed. Independent community banks face buyout pressure and competition from giants. The safeguards against that — deposit caps, antitrust law, Community Reinvestment Act evaluations — depend on regulators enforcing them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Community banks and their local customers

drawbacks.text: The bill lets holding companies acquire banks in a state 'whether or not' that state permits such acquisitions, so a state can no longer keep out-of-state companies from buying its banks outright.
A single company may lawfully hold up to a quarter of all deposits in a state, and the state supervisor can waive even that cap case by case, concentrating local banking in a few hands.

Consolidation of banking into a few large interstate companies reduces local ownership of banks and moves lending decisions away from the communities they serve; the bill's Community Reinvestment Act evaluations document lending but do not require it.
The Senate Banking Committee report carried additional views filed by committee members, signaling disagreement within the committee over the original measure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Interstate banking delivered real convenience — you can move and keep your bank — and the bill carried genuine safeguards: a 10% national deposit cap, a 25% state cap, antitrust preservation, host-state law over branches, and state-by-state community-lending evaluations. But the bill's central purpose was to free the largest banking companies to expand, and the decades of consolidation that followed left most places served by fewer, bigger banks. Ordinary people got convenience; local banking choice was the price.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate never voted on this bill as itself: it attached the bill's text to a House-passed vehicle, passed that version by voice vote, and then indefinitely postponed the shell of S. 1963.

narrative.text: The Senate Banking Committee ordered and reported this original measure on February 23 and March 23, 1994, with a written report and additional views, and it was placed on the Senate calendar.
The Senate took the bill up on April 25–26, 1994, laid it before the chamber by unanimous consent, and considered it over two days.

On April 26 the Senate incorporated this measure into H.R. 3841 as an amendment, passed H.R. 3841 in lieu of this measure by voice vote, and then indefinitely postponed S. 1963 by unanimous consent — so the bill itself never received a direct up-or-down vote.

The vehicle carrying these provisions became the Riegle-Neal Interstate Banking and Branching Efficiency Act of 1994, which President Clinton signed on September 29, 1994, legalizing interstate banking nationwide.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large bank holding companies came out ahead: they won nationwide acquisition and branching rights they had sought for years, and the safeguards in the law are the caps and evaluations written into this bill. Community banks lost ground to consolidation.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes are recorded — the Senate passed the measure by voice vote — and interstate banking drew active support from Democratic and Republican leaders alike, so the fight did not split by party.

industries.industry: Large bank holding companies and national banks
industries.note: The bill makes multistate banking companies the permanent structure of American banking, giving them the right to buy banks and open branches in any state. It regulates them at the same time — a 10% national and 25% state deposit cap, antitrust preservation, host-state consumer and fair-lending law, and Community Reinvestment Act evaluations in every state — but it locks in their gatekeeper role over where banking services come from.

Out-of-state companies can now buy their banks regardless of state refusal, and giants can branch into their markets. Their fate tracked their customers' interest in locally owned banking, and the industry warned of exactly the consolidation that followed.

industries.industry: State bank regulators and state governments
industries.note: States lose the power to bar out-of-state acquisitions, but the bill lets them tax out-of-state banks' shares, apply their consumer-protection and fair-lending laws to new branches, examine out-of-state branches, and opt out of some interstate combinations.
